steps.a:
- **Universal TOR rule - ALL THREE must be present:**
- → **Arrest NOT witnessed by EMS professionals**
- → **NO shock delivered**
- → **NO return of spontaneous circulation**
- Reasonable in a **TIERED EMS system with both ALS and BLS professionals**; prospectively validated there
- **Rule application depends on EMS SCOPE OF PRACTICE** - there are BLS, ALS and universal TOR rules
- **ETCO₂ should NOT be used in isolation** to end resuscitative efforts
- EMS systems **should be prepared to terminate resuscitation ON SCENE**, with training in death notification
bank_lines: Marrow: Traumatic arrest — resuscitative thoracotomy is for penetrating trauma with downtime <15 min (blunt <10 min); beyond ~20 min of CPR with no cardiac activity on echo, stop.

explain.sub: BLS & ACLS → Ending resuscitation → Termination rules
explain.intro: Step 6 ends with the decision to stop. Termination rules exist so that EMS teams stop where survival is near zero and transport where it is not. Three real questions test which rule fits which system, and one asks about traumatic arrest.
why: **Universal TOR rule: all three of arrest not witnessed by EMS, no shock delivered, no ROSC.** Together they identify arrests with very low survival: the arrest had already lasted an unknown time before EMS arrived, the rhythm was never shockable, and nothing has worked.
**Reasonable in a tiered EMS system with both ALS and BLS professionals; prospectively validated there.** AHA 2025 class 2a.

**The rule used depends on EMS scope of practice: BLS, ALS and universal rules.** The BLS rule (for BLS crews where ALS is not available) uses the same three criteria; the ALS rule adds ‘not witnessed by a bystander’ and ‘no bystander CPR’, so it is stricter, because ALS crews can offer more. None is validated for trauma, overdose or in-hospital arrest.

**ETCO₂ must not be used in isolation to stop.** In an intubated patient, ETCO₂ under 10 mmHg after 20 minutes of ALS may be one part of a multimodal decision; in a non-intubated patient no ETCO₂ cut-off should be used (class 3, harm), because mask leak and ventilation make it unreliable.
**EMS systems should be prepared to stop on scene, with training in death notification.** Transport with ongoing CPR is dangerous for crews and seldom saves a patient who meets the rule.
mimic: BLS vs ALS vs universal rule
BLS and universal: not EMS-witnessed, no shock, no ROSC. ALS: those three plus not bystander-witnessed and no bystander CPR.
Medical vs traumatic arrest

TOR rules are for medical OHCA. In trauma, resuscitative thoracotomy is for penetrating injury with CPR under about 15 minutes (blunt under 10); with no cardiac activity on echo after about 20 minutes, stop.
traps: “The BLS rule is the four- or five-criterion rule”
The card’s note has it backwards: the BLS rule has the same three criteria as the universal rule; the ALS rule adds the bystander criteria.
“TOR rules apply to traumatic arrest if criteria are met”
They are not validated in trauma.
“An isolated ETCO₂ threshold rule”
ETCO₂ is never used alone to stop.
decode: Tiered BLS/ALS system, OHCA — which TOR rule? [DocT GT ×2]
Universal TOR rule.
Penetrating chest trauma, asystole, 25 min downtime — management? [Marrow]
Echo; no cardiac motion → stop.
explain.punch: In a tiered EMS system use the universal rule: not EMS-witnessed, no shock, no ROSC, all three, then stop on scene. Never stop on ETCO₂ alone, and the rules do not apply to trauma.

explain.sub: Cardiology → ACLS → Arrest in pregnancy: principles
explain.intro: Step 4 opens the special circumstances with pregnancy. From about 20 weeks the uterus compresses the inferior vena cava and aorta when the woman lies supine, so CPR on her back produces even less output than usual. Three questions test that and the airway.
why: **Priorities: high-quality CPR and relief of aortocaval compression.** Compressions need venous return to fill the heart; a gravid uterus on the vena cava removes much of it.

**Continuous manual left lateral uterine displacement.** Pushing the uterus up and to the left lifts it off the vena cava while the woman stays flat, so compressions stay effective. A tilted board was used before, but tilting reduces compression force; AHA 2025 makes manual displacement class 1. It needs a second rescuer, which is the answer to the NEET recall.

**A difficult airway is common in pregnancy; use the most experienced provider; ETT or SGA; waveform capnography to confirm and monitor.** Airway oedema, breast tissue, a full stomach with a lax oesophageal sphincter and a lower functional residual capacity with higher oxygen demand mean she desaturates fast and aspirates easily. A cuffed tube protects the airway best, so it is the preferred device when an expert can place it.
**1 breath every 6 seconds (10/min) with continuous compressions once the advanced airway is in; team planning with obstetric, neonatal, emergency, anaesthesia, intensive care and arrest services.**
mimic: Manual uterine displacement vs left lateral tilt
Displacement keeps her flat for good compressions; tilt weakens them.
traps: “Half-dose epinephrine in pregnancy” or “avoid intubation until ROSC”
Drug doses are unchanged and the airway is secured early by the most experienced person.
“The second rescuer is needed for perimortem caesarean or defibrillation”
The second pair of hands is for continuous uterine displacement.
decode: 28 weeks, arrest in ICU — most critical ACLS modification? [DocT QBank]
Manual left uterine displacement (97%).
Preferred airway device in maternal arrest? [DocT QBank]
Endotracheal tube (92%).
Why is a second rescuer essential? [NEET 2025]
Uterine displacement.
explain.punch: In maternal arrest the uterus is the obstruction: push it left by hand while compressions continue, and let the most experienced person secure an airway that is both difficult and at risk of aspiration.

explain.sub: Cardiology → ACLS → Maternal arrest interventions and causes
explain.intro: Step 4 continues with what the maternal algorithm adds. Each addition answers a feature of pregnancy: the vena cava is blocked, the patient may be on magnesium, and the causes differ. Six questions test these, and two keys are disputed.
why: **Maternal: airway management • 100% O2, avoid excess ventilation • place IV above the diaphragm.** With the vena cava compressed, a drug given in a leg may not reach the heart; AHA 2025 recommends upper-limb IV or IO access.

**If receiving IV magnesium, stop it and give calcium chloride or gluconate.** Magnesium toxicity causes loss of reflexes, respiratory depression, conduction block and arrest; calcium antagonises its effect on the membrane. Hypermagnesaemia is the electrolyte cause to suspect when a woman on a magnesium infusion becomes bradycardic and arrests. Seizure prophylaxis can resume after ROSC.

**Obstetric: continuous lateral uterine displacement • detach fetal monitors • prepare for resuscitative delivery.** Fetal monitors are removed because they slow the move to delivery and interfere with defibrillation; the fetus is best served by restoring the mother’s circulation.

**Aetiologies A–H: anaesthetic complications, bleeding, cardiovascular, drugs, embolic, fever, general non-obstetric causes (H’s and T’s), hypertension.** Haemorrhage is the commonest single cause of maternal arrest, so PEA in pregnancy is treated as hypovolaemia first (wide-bore access above the diaphragm, massive transfusion, uterotonics, obstetrician to theatre). Drugs include magnesium toxicity and local anaesthetic toxicity; embolic includes amniotic fluid and pulmonary embolism.
mimic: Magnesium in eclampsia vs magnesium in arrest
Before arrest it is the treatment; once she arrests on an infusion it is a suspected cause: stop it and give calcium.
traps: “Give magnesium promptly as part of ACLS in eclampsia-related arrest” (DocT key, 68% chose it)
The algorithm says stop magnesium and give calcium; magnesium for seizures resumes after ROSC. If she was already on magnesium, choose calcium.
“Continue the magnesium infusion to prevent seizures, or delay changes until ROSC”
Stop it now and give calcium.
“Hypokalaemia or hypercalcaemia” for bradycardic arrest on the ICU (61% right)
On magnesium the suspect is hypermagnesaemia.
“Attach fetal monitors”
They are detached.
decode: PEA in pregnancy — commonest reversible cause? [DocT QBank]
Hypovolaemia from obstetric haemorrhage (81%).
Pregnant, bradycardia then arrest in ICU — electrolyte? [DocT QBank]
Hypermagnesaemia (61%).
Arrest on IV magnesium for pre-eclampsia, CPR and displacement under way — next? [DocT GT]
Stop magnesium, give IV calcium.

bank_lines: DocT: Evidence for resuscitative delivery is observational only: Katz, Dotters and Droegemueller 1986 (the '4-minute rule': start at 4 min, deliver by 5 min, because the gravid uterus cuts CPR output to ~30%), then Katz 2005 and Einav 2012 case reviews where ROSC often followed delivery. No RCT exists; MOMS = fetal myelomeningocele surgery, ALPS = late-preterm steroids, PROWESS = drotrecogin alfa.

DocT: Resuscitative hysterotomy uses a vertical midline incision from just above the symphysis to the umbilicus (fastest, best exposure), then a classical vertical uterine incision, done where the patient lies with CPR and uterine displacement continuing. Supra-umbilical or xiphoid incisions miss the uterus.

explain.sub: Cardiology → ACLS → Resuscitative delivery
explain.intro: Step 4 turns to delivery during arrest. Emptying the uterus relieves aortocaval compression, increases venous return and removes the fetus’s and placenta’s oxygen demand, so it is a manoeuvre for the mother first. Four questions test the timing, the evidence and the incision; two are poorly answered because they ask about trials.
why: **2025 term: resuscitative delivery, replacing ‘perimortem caesarean delivery’.** The new name says what it is for: maternal resuscitation, not fetal salvage.

**Preparation should begin at the recognition of cardiac arrest.** It is indicated when the fundus is at or above the umbilicus (about 20 weeks) and standard resuscitation has not restored circulation (class 1). The team, kit and operator are gathered from the first minute so that the clock is not lost.

**Goal: complete delivery by 5 minutes.** This comes from Katz, Dotters and Droegemueller (1986), the ‘4-minute rule’: start by 4 minutes, deliver by 5. It is a goal from case series, not a trial result. It is done where she lies, through a vertical midline incision from just above the symphysis to the umbilicus, with CPR and displacement continuing.
**Purpose: improve both maternal and fetal outcomes.** In case reviews (Katz 2005, Einav 2012) ROSC often followed delivery; earlier delivery was linked to better survival of both.

**ECPR is reasonable in pregnant or peripartum patients not responding to standard resuscitation (55% survival in the ELSO registry, 87% of 57 patients); a massive transfusion protocol with a balanced strategy, with tranexamic acid, for suspected amniotic fluid embolism (both class 1).** AHA 2025 gives the figures precisely: the 55% is survival among 42 obstetric patients given ECLS for cardiac arrest in the ELSO registry (for ECPR itself the registry figure was 29%), and the 87% is 30-day survival among 57 patients cannulated for arrest in pregnancy or within 24 hours of delivery. Pregnant patients are young, with reversible causes, which is why extracorporeal support does well. In AFE the typical sequence is sudden collapse with right heart failure, then consumptive coagulopathy and massive bleeding; AHA 2025 also supports VA-ECMO and inhaled pulmonary vasodilators.
mimic: Resuscitative delivery vs ordinary emergency caesarean
One is done at the bedside during CPR to resuscitate the mother; the other is done in theatre for maternal or fetal indications.
traps: “The HELP trial studied maternal arrest and perimortem caesarean” (DocT key; 14% right)

No such trial exists; the evidence is Katz 1986/2005 and Einav 2012. If Katz or a case series is offered, choose it; otherwise eliminate MOMS (fetal spina bifida surgery), ALPS (late-preterm steroids) and PROWESS (drotrecogin alfa in sepsis).
“After 20 minutes of failed CPR”, “only after fetal demise” or “after ROSC”
Prepare at recognition and deliver by 5 minutes if there is no ROSC.
“Supra-umbilical or xiphoid incision” (45% right)
Vertical midline from just above the symphysis to the umbilicus.

Origin of the ‘4-minute rule’ [DocT QBank]
Katz et al (54%).
Landmark for the incision [DocT QBank]

explain.punch: Resuscitative delivery is a manoeuvre for the mother: start preparing when the arrest is recognised, deliver by 5 minutes, and if that fails, extracorporeal support is reasonable.

**Condition** | **Recommendation**
**Asthma** | **ECLS** may be reasonable; **VOLATILE ANAESTHETICS** may be considered. Survival 83.5-100% in observational studies
**Hypothermia** | **ECLS for REWARMING**; use **prognostication scores (HOPE, ICE)** to guide initiation. May rewarm with ECLS if **core <28°C** even WITHOUT arrest

bank_lines: DocT + Marrow: Rewarm below the ECLS tier by stage: mild 32–35 °C passive external (dry, insulate; shivering adds ~1–2 °C/h; room-temperature fluid cools); moderate 28–32 °C active external (forced air) + IV fluid warmed to 38–42 °C; severe <28 °C or unstable = active internal (ECLS first, thoracic/peritoneal lavage if unavailable), which also counters afterdrop.

DocT: Hypothermic arrest <30 °C (ERC 2021): up to 3 shocks, then withhold further shocks, adrenaline and antiarrhythmics until core >30 °C (cold myocardium does not respond, drugs accumulate); at 30–35 °C double the drug interval (adrenaline every 6–10 min). Handle gently and keep horizontal — the cold heart is irritable and lidocaine does not work. AHA is more permissive; DocT keys ERC.

Marrow: In hypothermic arrest a serum K >12 mmol/L means massive cell lysis (asphyxia or death before cooling) — non-survivable, so stop CPR and do not start ECLS; fixed pupils and Osborn waves are unreliable for prognosis in the cold.

explain.sub: Cardiology → ACLS → Asthma, hypothermia and hyperthermia
explain.intro: Step 4 ends with the most-asked card in the deck: eleven questions, almost all on temperature. Cold and heat both kill, but in opposite ways: cold protects the brain and makes the heart unresponsive, so rewarming comes before drugs; heat injures every minute, so cooling speed is everything.
why: **Asthma: ECLS may be reasonable; volatile anaesthetics may be considered; survival 83.5–100% in observational studies.** Refractory asthma kills by gas trapping and hypercapnia, not by a damaged lung, so taking over gas exchange buys time for bronchodilators to work. Volatile agents relax bronchial smooth muscle directly.

**Hypothermia: ECLS for rewarming; prognostication scores (HOPE, ICE) to guide initiation; may rewarm with ECLS if core <28 °C even without arrest.** Below 28 °C the heart is prone to VF on handling. ECLS rewarms the core at 1.5–5 °C/h while supporting the circulation. HOPE estimates survival (under 10% predicts death) and is better than a potassium threshold alone; potassium above 12 mmol/L suggests cell lysis from asphyxia or death before cooling, and is non-survivable. Grades and rewarming: mild 32–35 °C passive external (dry, insulate; shivering rewarms); moderate 28–32 °C active external (forced air, warmed IV fluid); severe under 28 °C or unstable, active internal (ECLS, or thoracic or peritoneal lavage). The cold myocardium does not respond to shocks or drugs, and drugs accumulate: AHA 2025 now says defibrillate once and defer further shocks and epinephrine until 30 °C; ERC allows up to three shocks, withholds adrenaline below 30 °C and doubles its interval at 30–35 °C.

**Hyperthermia: ice water immersion (1–5 °C) preferred; cool as rapidly as possible, at least 0.15 °C/min.** Heat stroke (core over 40 °C with CNS dysfunction) damages cells in proportion to time above the critical temperature, so the outcome depends on how fast the core falls. Water conducts heat far better than air, which is why immersion beats fans, blankets and cold IV fluid. If ice water is not available, AHA 2025 accepts tepid water at 8–17 °C or tarp-assisted ice water; where immersion is not possible at all (frail elderly, ICU), evaporative cooling with ice packs is the fallback. Antipyretics do nothing because the set-point is normal, and dantrolene has no role outside malignant hyperthermia. AHA 2025 stops active cooling at 38.6 °C, because the core keeps falling after removal.
mimic: Hypothermic arrest vs normothermic arrest
Cold: rewarm, limit shocks and defer drugs below 30 °C, continue CPR long. Normothermic: standard ALS.
Heat stroke vs fever
Heat stroke has a normal set-point and needs physical cooling; fever responds to antipyretics.
traps: “Cool exertional heat stroke to at least 36 °C to prevent rebound” (DocT key; 78% chose it)
The key is wrong: stop cooling at about 38.6–39 °C (AHA 2025: 38.6 °C), because the core falls further after removal. Choose ‘stop at 39 °C’ if offered.
“Cooling blankets and fans” or “cold IV fluid alone” for heat stroke (59% right)
Ice-water immersion is fastest.
“Passive rewarming is wrong for mild hypothermia — use active external” (47% right)
Stable mild hypothermia needs only passive external rewarming.
“Give antiarrhythmics for VF at 29 °C” (53% right)

Continue CPR and withhold antiarrhythmics until above 30 °C; lidocaine does not work in a cold heart. ‘Defibrillate once and proceed with active rewarming’ is not wrong either (AHA 2025 allows one shock, ERC up to three), but the keyed answer is ‘continue CPR and withhold antiarrhythmics’.
“AHA is more permissive than ERC on shocks and drugs in hypothermia”
That was AHA 2020; AHA 2025 defers further shocks and epinephrine below 30 °C, close to ERC.

b Who is a candidate
c The time target

steps.a:
a **Venoarterial**, always - the patient has no cardiac output, so a venous return would circulate nothing.
b Refractory arrest with witnessed onset, bystander CPR, an initial shockable rhythm or another reversible cause, a younger patient with few comorbidities, and definitive treatment immediately available - PCI, thrombectomy, rewarming.
c Low-flow time as short as possible; most programmes target cannulation within 60 minutes of the arrest.
d Unwitnessed arrest, prolonged low-flow time without CPR, known terminal illness, severe aortic regurgitation, uncontrolled bleeding.
bank_lines: DocT GT: Surugadai (Tokyo) ECPR criteria exclude a presumed non-cardiac cause, ROSC within 10 min of arrival, core temperature <30 °C and pregnancy; a core temperature of 30–35 °C is NOT an exclusion (hypothermia is a favourable reversible cause).

explain.sub: Cardiology → ECPR → Configuration, selection, timing, exclusions
explain.intro: Step 5 applies VA ECMO to a heart that has stopped. The trials show it helps only when the right patient reaches the circuit quickly, with a fix waiting. The one real question tested the Surugadai criteria, and only 42% saw that a core temperature under 35 °C is not an exclusion.
why: **Venoarterial, always.** With no cardiac output, blood returned to a vein would sit in a still heart; only arterial return perfuses the body.

**Candidate: witnessed arrest, bystander CPR, initial shockable rhythm or another reversible cause, younger with few comorbidities, and a definitive treatment ready (PCI, thrombectomy, rewarming).** Each criterion shortens the no-flow time or predicts a heart and brain that can recover. AHA 2025 makes ECPR reasonable ‘in select patients when provided within an appropriately trained and equipped system of care’ (2a) but sets no fixed criteria; ELSO’s 2021 interim guideline uses age under 70, witnessed arrest, a shockable rhythm, no-flow under 5 minutes and low-flow under 60 minutes, and states these are consensus, not validated.

**Low-flow time as short as possible; most target cannulation within 60 minutes of arrest.** Neurologically intact survival falls steeply with each minute of conventional CPR. ARREST (30 patients, refractory VF, a mobile cath-lab system) showed survival to discharge of 43% vs 7% and stopped early; Prague OHCA (264 patients) gave 31.5% vs 22.0% good neurological survival at 180 days (not significant); INCEPTION (160 randomised, 134 analysed, 10 Dutch centres) gave 20% vs 16% at 30 days (not significant). The benefit appears only in fast, experienced systems.

**Exclusions: unwitnessed arrest, long no-flow time, terminal illness, severe aortic regurgitation, uncontrolled bleeding.** Aortic regurgitation lets retrograde ECMO flow fill the LV; bleeding forbids the heparin the circuit needs; aortic dissection is also an exclusion.
mimic: Hypothermia 30–35 °C vs below 30 °C (Surugadai)
Mild to moderate hypothermia is a protective, reversible state and favours ECPR; only a core temperature under 30 °C is listed as an exclusion.
traps: “Core temperature under 35 °C excludes ECPR” (42% right)
In the Surugadai criteria, as DocT quotes them, the exclusions are presumed non-cardiac cause, ROSC within 10 minutes of arrival, core temperature under 30 °C and pregnancy; 30–35 °C is not excluded.
“ROSC within 10 minutes is a reason to cannulate”
It is an exclusion: the patient no longer has a refractory arrest.

explain.punch: ECPR is VA ECMO started in a refractory arrest so that a reversible cause can be fixed; it works only when the patient is well chosen and on the circuit within about an hour.

explain.intro: Step 6 leaves arrest for the patient who may arrest next. In ACS the ECG sorts patients in minutes into those who need reperfusion now and those who need a troponin pathway. The one real question, a T-wave inversion with pain, was answered right by only 44%.
why: **Prehospital: support ABCs and monitor ECG • obtain and evaluate a 12-lead ECG • consider IV access, oxygen, aspirin, nitrate, morphine • transfer to an emergency PCI-capable facility.** A prehospital ECG lets the cath lab be activated before arrival. Oxygen only if SpO2 is under 90%; giving it to normoxic patients does not help (AVOID, DETO2X).

explain.sub: Post-arrest care → Immediate post-ROSC algorithm
explain.intro: Step 4 is the first minutes after ROSC. The card follows the AHA adult post-arrest algorithm, with two parallel branches: the ECG decides on the cath lab, the conscious level decides on temperature control. The one bank question tests the second branch.
why: **Step 2: optimise ventilation and oxygenation — SpO₂ 90–98% (PaO₂ 60–105 mmHg; avoid hypoxaemia and hyperoxia), consider an advanced airway, waveform capnography, do not hyperventilate.** Hypoxaemia extends the ischaemic injury; very high PaO₂ feeds free-radical injury. Capnography confirms tube position and guards against hyperventilation, which constricts cerebral vessels and raises intrathoracic pressure.

**Step 3: treat hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg) with an IV/IO bolus, a vasopressor infusion and a search for treatable causes.** The brain after arrest has lost autoregulation, so its flow follows pressure. AHA 2025 frames the target as MAP at least 65 mmHg rather than an SBP threshold (PCA-17).

**Step 4: 12-lead ECG — STEMI or high suspicion of AMI → yes: step 5, coronary reperfusion.** ST elevation after ROSC means an occluded artery until proved otherwise, and angiography is emergent whether or not the patient is awake (PCA-18).

**Step 6: follows commands? No → step 7, targeted temperature management.** Not following commands is the marker of brain injury, and it is the only entry criterion: rhythm and cause do not matter (AHA 2025, COR 1). Temperature is now held at 32–37.5 °C for at least 36 hours.
**Yes at step 6 → step 8, advanced critical care.** A patient who follows commands has no brain injury to protect with temperature control but still needs the cause treated and the organs supported.

explain.sub: ACLS → Post-cardiac arrest → 2025 targets
explain.intro: Step 4 is the hours after ROSC, when the brain is exposed to secondary injury from low pressure, abnormal gases and fever. The questions test whether the old 32–34 °C answer still stands.
why: **MAP ≥65 mmHg; avoid hypotension.** The brain after arrest has impaired autoregulation, so flow follows pressure; AHA 2025 dropped the old SBP target because the trials used MAP (1). Higher MAP targets (BOX, NEUROPROTECT) did not improve outcome.

**SpO₂ 90–98% (PaO₂ 60–105 mmHg); 100% FiO₂ until SpO₂ can be measured reliably.** Hypoxia worsens brain injury, and hyperoxia adds free-radical injury on reperfusion, so FiO₂ is titrated down once the saturation reads reliably.
**PaCO₂ 35–45 mmHg.** Low CO₂ constricts cerebral vessels and lowers flow to an ischaemic brain; high CO₂ raises ICP. Hyperventilation is to be avoided.

**Temperature control for at least 36 hours in patients unresponsive to verbal commands; goal 32–37.5 °C.** TTM (33 vs 36 °C) and TTM2 (33 vs normothermia with fever prevention, ≤37.5 °C) showed no difference in survival or neurological outcome, so AHA 2025 accepts any deliberate target in this range. The essential element is preventing fever, which worsens injury. ERC–ESICM 2025 recommend actively preventing fever (target 37.5 °C or less) for 36–72 hours in patients who remain comatose (the 2021 version said 37.7 °C or less for at least 72 hours).

**Coronary angiography before discharge in survivors with suspected cardiac cause, especially an initial shockable rhythm, unexplained LV dysfunction or severe ischaemia.** Emergent angiography is for persistent ST elevation; without it, immediate angiography did not help (COACT, TOMAHAWK).

why: **Airway; stomach decompression (NG/OG tube).** Bag-mask ventilation during CPR fills the stomach with air; decompressing it reduces aspiration and splinting of the diaphragm.
**Lung-protective ventilation.** Low tidal volume (about 6–8 mL/kg predicted body weight) because aspiration and reperfusion injure the lung and ARDS is common (PCA-03).

**PaCO₂ 35–45 mmHg.** In AHA 2025 and ERC–ESICM 2025. Hypocapnia constricts cerebral vessels and cuts flow to an ischaemic brain; hypercapnia raises ICP. CO₂ is checked on a blood gas rather than trusted to the capnograph, and it is checked often during cooling, because lower temperature cuts CO₂ production and an unchanged ventilator setting then drifts the patient into hypocapnia.

**Saturation 90–98% (PaO₂ 60–105 mmHg; AHA 2025).** ERC keeps 94–98% (PaO₂ 75–100). The BOX trial’s two oxygen targets (PaO₂ 68–75 vs 98–105 mmHg) gave the same outcome, so the safe zone is broad; the danger is at the extremes.

**Avoid hyperventilation and hyperoxia.** Hyperventilation: cerebral vasoconstriction plus higher intrathoracic pressure, less venous return and lower output. Hyperoxia: more free-radical injury in freshly reperfused tissue. Hypoxia is avoided too, because it repeats the original insult.

steps.a:
- **Arterial and central lines**
- **MAP >65**, **SBP >90**, **urine output 0.5-1 mL/kg/hr** → **to optimise CEREBRAL PERFUSION**
- **12-lead ECG** to rule out MI • **ECHO and critical care USG screening**
- **Fluid only if volume-responsive** (isotonic crystalloid in small boluses, reassessed on echo); no fixed 20-30 mL/kg load
- **Vasopressors: noradrenaline first** (ERC-ESICM 2025; AHA 2025: no specific agent proven, class 2b) • dobutamine if the stunned pump is the problem
- **Mechanical support: IABP, ECMO, IMPELLA** • immunomodulation

explain.sub: Post-arrest care → ICU → Haemodynamic targets
explain.intro: Step 6 continues with pressure. The brain after arrest has lost autoregulation (PCA-03), so a perfusing pressure is a brain treatment. The only Grand Test question on this card was answered right by 24%, because DocT keyed a MAP higher than any guideline recommends.
why: **Arterial and central lines.** Beat-to-beat pressure because vasopressors are titrated minute to minute; central access for the vasopressors and ScvO₂.

**MAP >65, SBP >90, urine output 0.5–1 mL/kg/h, to optimise cerebral perfusion.** AHA 2025 confirms MAP at least 65 mmHg (COR 1); ERC–ESICM 2025 says MAP >60–65 or SBP >100. A higher target has been tested and did not help: BOX (2022) compared MAP 63 and 77 mmHg in comatose survivors and found no difference in death or severe disability.

**12-lead ECG to rule out MI; echo and critical care ultrasound screening.** Echo shows whether shock is cardiogenic (poor LV), distributive (good LV, low SVR) or obstructive (tamponade, RV dilatation).

**Fluid only if volume-responsive (isotonic crystalloid in small boluses, reassessed on echo); no fixed 20–30 mL/kg load.** The stunned ventricle cannot handle large volumes, and extra fluid worsens the lung injury.

**Vasopressors: noradrenaline first (ERC–ESICM 2025; AHA 2025: no specific agent proven, 2b); dobutamine if the stunned pump is the problem; mechanical support: IABP, ECMO, Impella; immunomodulation.** ERC–ESICM 2025 actually says ‘fluids, noradrenaline and/or dobutamine’ according to need without ranking a first agent (FLAGS); noradrenaline is the usual first choice in practice. AHA 2025 says temporary mechanical support should not be used routinely (3: No Benefit) but may be considered in selected refractory cardiogenic shock (2b); see CS-49 to CS-52.
mimic: Post-arrest MAP target vs TBI or spinal cord targets
Post-arrest: at least 65 mmHg. Higher MAP goals (85–90 mmHg) belong to acute spinal cord injury, and TBI is managed by cerebral perfusion pressure; neither applies to post-arrest care.
traps: “Comatose, on TTM, MAP 65 despite fluids: increase MAP to >80 mmHg” (DocT key, 24% right)

No guideline supports this: AHA 2025 and ERC–ESICM target MAP ≥65, and BOX found no benefit from a higher MAP. The DocT key is wrong; if the stem is DocT’s, pick >80, but on a guideline-framed question keep ≥65.
“Rewarm rapidly” or “stop TTM because of STEMI”
Rapid rewarming causes rebound hypotension and fever; STEMI and temperature control run together (PCA-18).
“Delay reperfusion until awakening”
STEMI goes to the cath lab regardless of coma.
decode: Comatose post-arrest on TTM, day 1, MAP 65 despite fluids: next step? [DocT GT, 24%]
DocT key: increase MAP >80. Guideline answer: MAP ≥65 is already the target (FLAGS).
[pattern] Post-ROSC MAP target
At least 65 mmHg (AHA 2025); >60–65 (ERC–ESICM 2025).
explain.punch: After arrest the pressure target exists for the brain, and it is a MAP of at least 65: BOX found nothing gained by pushing to 77, so a key that demands over 80 is DocT’s, not the guideline’s.

steps.q:
**Give:**
a The five components of arrhythmia management post-arrest
b The four indications for coronary angiography
c When TTM can be initiated
d What else is started in appropriate patients
steps.a:
- **Arrhythmias:** anti-arrhythmics • **correct electrolyte imbalance** • treat coronary ischaemia • **toxin management** • **temperature correction**
- **Emergent angiogram ± PCI (AHA 2025):** **persistent ST elevation**, comatose or not (COR 1) • reasonable without STE if **cardiogenic shock, recurrent ventricular arrhythmias or ongoing ischaemia** (COR 2a) • otherwise **not** emergent: no benefit over a delayed strategy (COR 3; COACT, TOMAHAWK)
- **TTM can be initiated DURING the angiogram**
- **ACS medical management** should be started in appropriate patients

explain.sub: Post-arrest care → Arrhythmias and coronary angiography
explain.intro: Step 5 returns to the commonest cause, the coronary artery. The two bank questions both turn on one rule: ST elevation after ROSC goes to the cath lab now, whatever the neurological state. Half the Grand Test cohort chose to wait.
why: **Arrhythmias: anti-arrhythmics, correct electrolyte imbalance, treat coronary ischaemia, toxin management, temperature correction.** Post-arrest arrhythmias are mostly secondary, so the cause is treated: potassium and magnesium, ischaemia (reperfusion), drugs, and temperature (cooling causes bradycardia; rewarming and fever cause tachyarrhythmias).

**Emergent angiogram ± PCI (AHA 2025): persistent ST elevation, comatose or not (COR 1); reasonable without STE if cardiogenic shock, recurrent ventricular arrhythmias or ongoing ischaemia (2a); otherwise not emergent, no benefit over a delayed strategy (3; COACT, TOMAHAWK).** In COACT (552 patients with shockable arrest and no ST elevation) 90-day survival was 64.5% with immediate and 67.2% with delayed angiography; TOMAHAWK found no benefit either. ERC–ESICM 2025 agrees: emergent cath lab for persistent STE, otherwise delay unless acute occlusion is likely.
**TTM can be initiated during the angiogram.** The two treatments are independent and should not delay each other.
**ACS medical management should be started in appropriate patients.** Antiplatelets, anticoagulation and statin as for any ACS, adjusted for bleeding risk from CPR and for cooling.
mimic: PCI vs thrombolysis after ROSC with STEMI
Primary PCI is preferred; prolonged or traumatic CPR is a relative contraindication to fibrinolysis, which is kept for when PCI cannot be done in time.
traps: “Wait for a favourable neurological prognosis, or correct the metabolic derangement first” (50% right)
Coma is not a reason to delay: AHA 2025 recommends emergent angiography for STE regardless of coma (COR 1). Metabolic problems are corrected in the lab, not before.
“Angiography within 24–48 hours”
That is the timing for patients without STE; with STE it is emergent.
“Thrombolysis” for post-ROSC STEMI
Primary PCI is the answer when available; CPR raises the bleeding risk of lysis.
“No obvious cause, so emergent angiography”
No longer an indication without STE, shock, recurrent arrhythmia or ischaemia (COACT, TOMAHAWK).
decode: VF arrest after snow shovelling, ROSC, mental status not determinable, post-ROSC ECG shown: timing of angiography? [DocT GT, 50%]
Urgently post-ROSC (the ECG shows STEMI).
VF arrest, ROSC, anterior ST elevation, haemodynamically unstable: next step? [NEET 2025 recall]
Immediate coronary angiography with PCI.
[pattern] Comatose after shockable arrest, no STE, stable: emergency angiography?
No: delayed or selective strategy is as good.
explain.punch: Persistent ST elevation after ROSC means the cath lab now, comatose or not, with temperature control started on the table; without ST elevation angiography waits unless there is shock, recurrent arrhythmia or ongoing ischaemia.

steps.q:
**For seizures and myoclonus after ROSC, give:**
a The % of comatose patients affected, and the % with myoclonus
b Their prognostic significance
c The evidence for seizure prophylaxis, and the first-line agents
d Which drug is inefficient for myoclonus, and the four agents that are used
steps.a:
- Seizures occur in **33%** of comatose patients after ROSC; **myoclonus is more common: 20-25%**
- Both are **POOR PROGNOSTIC MARKERS**; cerebral oedema is a consequence of hypoxic brain injury
- **Management**
- **Seizures** | **NO sufficient evidence for PROPHYLAXIS**; **EEG to monitor treatment effects**; **levetiracetam or sodium valproate first line**
- **Myoclonus** | **PHENYTOIN IS INEFFICIENT**; use **propofol, sodium valproate, clonazepam, levetiracetam**

explain.sub: Post-arrest care → ICU → Seizures and myoclonus
explain.intro: Step 6 includes the brain’s electrical response to hypoxic injury. Both Grand Test questions here are about the comatose patient with seizures or myoclonus: what it means for prognosis, and what to do when an EEG pattern persists.
why: **Seizures occur in 33% of comatose patients after ROSC; myoclonus is more common, 20–25%.** The two figures come from the ERC post-resuscitation text (2015, repeated in 2021): seizures in about one-third of patients who stay comatose, and myoclonus the commonest type, in 18–25%. So 20–25% is a subset of the 33%; ‘more common’ means the commonest form, not more frequent than seizures overall. ILCOR 2008 gives 10–40% for seizures, myoclonus or both in comatose survivors. Myoclonus is the commonest visible form, while many other seizures are seen only on EEG.

**Both are poor prognostic markers; cerebral oedema is a consequence of hypoxic brain injury.** Early generalised myoclonus, especially status myoclonus within 72 hours with a burst-suppression EEG, reflects severe cortical injury; ERC–ESICM 2025 lists status myoclonus ≤72 h among its poor-outcome predictors. It is never used alone (multimodal prognosis), and late action myoclonus in an awakening patient (Lance–Adams syndrome) has a good outlook.

**Seizures: no sufficient evidence for prophylaxis; EEG to monitor treatment effects; levetiracetam or sodium valproate first line.** AHA 2025 and ERC–ESICM 2025 both advise against routine prophylaxis (no trial benefit); ERC–ESICM names levetiracetam or sodium valproate as first line, with sedatives such as propofol, and AHA 2025 asks for clinical seizures to be treated without naming an agent. TELSTAR (2022) found that aggressively suppressing rhythmic and periodic EEG patterns did not change the poor outcome (about 90% in both arms), so treating the EEG does not rescue the prognosis.

**Myoclonus: phenytoin is inefficient; use propofol, sodium valproate, clonazepam, levetiracetam.** Post-anoxic myoclonus is cortical and subcortical, not the type phenytoin controls. AHA 2025: get an EEG, and do not treat myoclonus that has no EEG correlate (3: No Benefit); ERC–ESICM 2025 suggests a wake-up trial when the EEG background is benign.
mimic: Myoclonic status vs Lance–Adams
Comatose and early with a malignant EEG vs awake and later with action-triggered jerks.
Seizure vs shivering under TTM
Shivering is rhythmic muscle activity without EEG change and stops with warming of the skin, magnesium or deeper sedation.
traps: “EEG activity means a high chance of recovery”
Rhythmic, malignant EEG activity with myoclonus points the other way (84% right).
“Oxcarbazepine and topiramate are the only proven agents”
No drug has proven benefit; first line is levetiracetam or valproate, with propofol and clonazepam.
“Lumbar puncture is essential”
Post-anoxic myoclonus after a long arrest needs EEG and multimodal assessment, not an LP.
“Pattern persists after propofol and valproate: wait, or stop sedation” (69% right)

Seizure activity persisting on two agents is escalated by adding another, levetiracetam; waiting or withdrawing sedation leaves it running. TELSTAR shows that suppressing the EEG pattern does not improve outcome, so escalation treats the seizure, not the prognosis.
“Phenytoin for post-anoxic myoclonus”
Ineffective.
decode: Alcohol-using woman after OHCA and 24 h hypothermia, rapid face and limb twitching after rewarming, EEG rhythmic activity: most true? [DocT GT, 84%]
Post-anoxic myoclonic status epilepticus indicates a poor prognosis.
Comatose post-arrest, malignant epileptiform EEG persisting 90 min on propofol and valproate: next step? [DocT GT, 69%]
Add levetiracetam.
[pattern] Seizure prophylaxis after ROSC?
Not recommended.
explain.punch: Seizures and early myoclonus are common after arrest and signal severe injury; there is no prophylaxis, levetiracetam or valproate with propofol come first, phenytoin does not work for myoclonus, and myoclonus without an EEG correlate is not treated.

**comatose patients**
a **MAP ≥ 65, SBP ≥ 90 mmHg.**
b **SpO2 90–98% (PaO2 60–105); PaCO2 35–45.**

bank_lines: Marrow: Poor-prognosis signs after arrest (multimodal, ≥72 h): status epilepticus or myoclonic status during temperature control, bilaterally absent pupillary and corneal reflexes, high NSE, burst suppression on EEG, sustained upgaze. Absent arm movement with preserved legs may be man-in-a-barrel (watershed infarct) and is not always poor; a brief 3–5 min arrest can recover fully.

Marrow: Rewarm after temperature control at ~0.25 °C/h on an automated device (about 16 h for 4 °C) and never faster than 0.5 °C/h; rapid rewarming causes vasodilatory hypotension, potassium shifts and rebound fever.

explain.sub: Cardiology → Post-ROSC → Targets for the comatose survivor
explain.intro: After ROSC the heart has restarted, but the outcome is decided by the brain. Every target on this card protects a brain that has lost autoregulation and is primed for secondary injury.
why: **MAP ≥65, SBP ≥90 mmHg.** Without autoregulation, cerebral flow follows pressure, so hypotension adds ischaemia. AHA 2025 now gives only MAP ≥65 mmHg (COR 1) and has dropped the SBP target; no particular vasopressor is recommended. Higher MAP targets (BOX, NEUROPROTECT) did not improve outcome.

**SpO₂ 90–98% (PaO₂ 60–105); PaCO₂ 35–45.** 100% oxygen until saturation can be measured reliably, then titrate down: hypoxaemia kills neurons, while hyperoxia adds free radicals at reperfusion. Low CO₂ constricts cerebral vessels and reduces flow; high CO₂ raises ICP. Pulse oximetry can overestimate in darker skin.

**32–37.5 °C, any rhythm, any location; at least 36 h (2025); rewarm no faster than 0.5 °C/h; prevent fever.** TTM-2 found no difference between 33 °C and normothermia with active fever prevention, so the range is wide; what matters is avoiding fever, which increases neuronal death. It applies to every patient who does not follow commands, including PEA, asystole and in-hospital arrest. Rewarming is slow because a fast rise raises cerebral metabolic demand while oxygen delivery is still fragile, and causes vasodilatory hypotension and rebound hyperkalaemia as potassium moves out of cells. An automated device at about 0.25 °C/h takes about 16 hours for 4 °C; manual rewarming takes about 24 hours (Marrow).

**Seizure ≥10 min continuous, or seizures for ≥20% of any 60 min.** This is the ACNS 2021 definition of electrographic status epilepticus. AHA 2025: prompt EEG in all who do not follow commands; treat clinical seizures; no routine prophylaxis. Status epilepticus persisting at or beyond 72 h, burst suppression off sedation, bilaterally absent pupillary and corneal reflexes at ≥72 h, absent N20 SSEPs and high NSE support a poor outcome, only in a multimodal assessment at least 72 hours after normothermia.

**STEMI, or cardiogenic shock / suspected coronary cause — not everyone.** Emergent angiography for ST elevation (COR 1); reasonable for shock, recurrent ventricular arrhythmias or ongoing ischaemia (2a). For comatose patients without these, COACT and TOMAHAWK found no benefit from immediate angiography over a delayed approach (COR 3).
mimic: Post-arrest rewarming vs accidental hypothermia afterdrop
Post-arrest: slow rewarming to protect the brain. Afterdrop (core temperature falling as cold peripheral blood returns) belongs to accidental hypothermia.
traps: “Strict 32–34 °C” or “PEA excluded from temperature control”
Outdated: 32–37.5 °C for all comatose patients, any rhythm (GT4 Q60).
“36 °C for 12 h”
At least 36 hours of temperature control (the GT4 miss).
“Slow rewarming prevents a fall in potassium and post-rewarming diuresis”
Rewarming RAISES potassium; the main reason is cerebral metabolic demand outstripping delivery (only 45% chose that).
“No upper-limb motor response always means a poor outcome”
Absent or extensor arm response is of uncertain value; arms weak with legs moving may be a watershed (man-in-a-barrel) injury, and a short arrest can recover fully.
decode: Rationale for slow controlled rewarming after therapeutic hypothermia [DocT QBank, 45%]
Rapid rewarming abruptly raises cerebral metabolic demand → secondary brain injury.
Post-arrest coma: finding most specific for poor prognosis [Marrow]
Status epilepticus during active cooling (with other signs, at ≥72 h).
Rewarming 33 → 37 °C with ice packs, no automated device — timeframe? [Marrow]
About 24 hours.
Revived after 20 min arrest — NOT true [Marrow]
‘No upper-limb motor response always means poor outcome’.
explain.punch: After ROSC keep MAP ≥65, SpO₂ 90–98% and PaCO₂ 35–45, control temperature at 32–37.5 °C for at least 36 h in every comatose patient, rewarm at ≤0.5 °C/h, and take only STEMI or shock straight to the lab.

steps.q:
**Name the 2025 changes to post-cardiac arrest care covering:**
a Blood pressure
b Temperature control duration and range
c Oxygenation
d Diagnostic imaging
e Myoclonus
f Neuroprognostication
g Recovery and survivorship
steps.a:
- **MAP ≥65 mmHg**; four RCTs showed no benefit from higher targets
- **Temperature control for AT LEAST 36 HOURS, goal 32-37.5°C** (was ≥24 h at 32-36°C)
- **SpO2 90-98% (PaO2 60-105 mmHg)**; PCO2 35-45 unchanged
- **HEAD-TO-PELVIS CT** and **echocardiography / POCUS** may be reasonable after ROSC
- **Do NOT treat myoclonus WITHOUT an EEG correlate**
- **Prognostication now includes predictors of FAVOURABLE outcome**; **NEUROFILAMENT LIGHT CHAIN** added as a biomarker
- **Temporary MCS** may be considered in refractory post-arrest cardiogenic shock
- **Structured assessment and referral for emotional distress in SURVIVORS AND CAREGIVERS** before discharge
- Avoid glucose **<70 and >180 mg/dL**

explain.sub: Cardiology → Post-cardiac arrest care → AHA 2025 changes
explain.intro: Step 3 follows the patient into the ICU. The post-arrest numbers changed more than any others in 2025, mostly because large trials (TTM2, BOX and the MAP-target trials) showed that more aggressive targets did not help. Both DocT Grand Test questions test temperature control: its duration and its range.
why: **MAP ≥65 mmHg; four RCTs showed no benefit from higher targets. Temporary MCS may be considered in refractory post-arrest cardiogenic shock.** MAP ≥65 is class 1. Four trials (over 1,000 OHCA patients) compared MAP targets around 65–70 with higher ones and found no difference in survival or neurological outcome, so the separate systolic target of 2020 (SBP ≥90) was dropped. Temporary MCS is 2b for highly selected refractory shock; routine use is 3: No Benefit because it added bleeding and ischaemic harm without survival gain.

**Temperature control for AT LEAST 36 HOURS, goal 32–37.5 °C (was ≥24 h at 32–36 °C).** TTM2 (2021) found no difference between 33 °C and normothermia with active fever prevention, so the range now runs up to 37.5 °C and both strategies count as temperature control (32–37.5 °C, class 1). Strictly, that wider range first appeared in the AHA 2023 focused update; the 2025 change is that the range is now joined to a 36-hour minimum. The minimum duration is 36 hours (2a), because the fever that follows early rewarming is linked to worse outcomes. Rewarm no faster than 0.5 °C/h (2b). ERC–ESICM 2025 frames the same idea as active fever prevention (≤37.5 °C) for 36–72 hours; the ‘>37.7 °C for 72 hours’ wording is their 2021 version.

**SpO2 90–98% (PaO2 60–105 mmHg); PCO2 35–45 unchanged. Avoid glucose <70 and >180 mg/dL.** Give 100% oxygen until saturation can be measured reliably (1), then titrate to 90–98% (2a); 2020 used 92–98%. BOX (2022) compared a PaO2 target of 68–75 with 98–105 mmHg and found no difference, so the lower floor is safe, and hyperoxia is avoided. PaCO2 35–45 (1) keeps cerebral blood flow normal; TAME showed no benefit from mild hypercapnia. Glucose: avoid the extremes (2b), with no tighter target. ERC–ESICM 2025 keeps 94–98%.

**HEAD-TO-PELVIS CT and echocardiography / POCUS may be reasonable after ROSC.** Both are new 2b statements. CT finds the cause (subarachnoid haemorrhage, pulmonary embolism, dissection) and the injuries of CPR (rib and sternal fractures, liver tears, pneumothorax), with a yield near 30%. Echo finds tamponade, RV strain, regional wall motion loss and LV failure that change treatment. A 12-lead ECG as soon as feasible stays class 1.

**Do NOT treat myoclonus WITHOUT an EEG correlate.** New: 3: No Benefit, because there is no evidence that non-epileptic myoclonus adds brain injury, and suppressing it needs sedatives that cloud the neurological examination. Myoclonus should prompt an EEG (1); clinical seizures are treated (1), non-convulsive seizures reasonably (2a), and prophylaxis is not given (3).

**Prognostication now includes predictors of FAVOURABLE outcome; NEUROFILAMENT LIGHT CHAIN added as a biomarker.** See ACLS-70 for the detail: a continuous EEG background without discharges, normal NSE or a withdrawal motor response now support a good outcome, and NfL joins NSE as a marker of poor outcome.

**Structured assessment and referral for emotional distress in SURVIVORS AND CAREGIVERS before discharge.** Anxiety, depression and post-traumatic stress are common in both, so 2025 asks for a structured screen and referral after stabilisation and before discharge; the chain’s last link, recovery, starts in hospital.
mimic: Temperature control vs therapeutic hypothermia
Temperature control is the umbrella (32–37.5 °C); hypothermia (32–34 °C) is one way of doing it.
AHA vs ERC–ESICM post-ROSC oxygen
traps: “Temperature control for at least 24 hours” (2020)
2025 says at least 36 hours.
“Strict hypothermia at 32–34 °C for 72 hours”
Neither the range nor the duration: any target within 32–37.5 °C for at least 36 hours.
“Avoid temperature control unless seizures develop”
Protocolised temperature control is class 1 for every patient who does not follow commands after ROSC.
“Temperature control goal 32–35 °C is a component of post-arrest care”
That range belongs to no guideline; 2025 is 32–37.5 °C, so this is the option that is not a component, while MAP ≥65, PCO2 35–45 and EEG in the non-commanding patient all are.

Temperature control for at least 36 hours.
Which is not a component of post-arrest care — MAP ≥65, PCO2 35–45, temperature 32–35 °C, EEG if not following commands? [DocT GT]

explain.punch: Post-arrest care in 2025 is less aggressive in its targets but longer and broader in its reach: oxygen down to 90%, MAP 65, any temperature from 32 to 37.5 °C held for 36 hours, and imaging and prognosis that look for every cause and every chance.

steps.q:
**Give the beneficial effects of therapeutic hypothermia relating to:**
a Its overall purpose
b The three metabolic reductions
c The two neurotransmitters whose release is inhibited
d The mechanism by which apoptosis is inhibited
steps.a:
- **Limits neurologic injury after resuscitation from cardiac arrest**
- **Reduction in BRAIN METABOLISM**
**Reduction in OXYGEN UTILISATION**
**Reduction in ATP CONSUMPTION**
- **Inhibits the release of GLUTAMATE and DOPAMINE**
- **Inhibits APOPTOSIS** - by reduction in **calcium overload** and **glutamate release**

explain.sub: Post-arrest care → Temperature control → Why cooling protects (mechanisms 1)
explain.intro: Step 1 explains why anyone tried cooling the brain after arrest. The damage done after ROSC (the post-cardiac-arrest brain injury) runs on temperature-dependent chemistry, so cooling slows it down. The DocT question that only half the cohort got right tests whether you see this as many mechanisms together or as one.
why: **Purpose: to limit neurological injury after resuscitation from cardiac arrest.** The heart is restarted, but the brain keeps being damaged for hours to days by secondary injury. Temperature control is aimed only at that secondary injury, which is why it is offered to patients who are not following commands (they are the ones with a brain at risk).

**Reduces brain metabolism, oxygen use and ATP consumption.** Cerebral metabolic rate falls by roughly 6–10% for each degree Celsius of cooling, so the brain needs less oxygen and burns less ATP while its blood flow is still unreliable. This is the Marrow answer to ‘rationale after VF arrest’: reduced cerebral oxygen consumption. It is real but modest; mild cooling protects more than the metabolic fall alone would explain, which is why part c and d matter.

**Inhibits the release of glutamate and dopamine.** Ischaemia floods the synapse with excitatory amino acids, glutamate opens NMDA channels and calcium pours into neurones (excitotoxicity). Cooling reduces this release, so fewer neurones are pushed into the calcium overload of part d.

**Inhibits apoptosis, by reducing calcium overload and glutamate release.** Calcium overload activates the enzymes and mitochondrial pathways that trigger programmed cell death in the days after arrest. Less glutamate means less calcium entry, and less calcium means fewer neurones enter that pathway.
mimic: Single mechanism vs combination

Every single-mechanism option (‘primarily metabolic’, ‘primarily vasoconstriction’, ‘selectively apoptosis’) is wrong; the correct option always names several pathways (reperfusion, excitotoxins, blood-brain barrier).
traps: “Hypothermia primarily reduces metabolism linearly and uniformly across the brain”
Metabolism does fall, but neither linearly nor uniformly, and it is not the whole story; this was the most chosen wrong option when only 50% were right.
“The primary benefit is cerebral vasoconstriction that lowers ICP”
Cerebral blood flow falls because metabolism falls (coupling), not as the protective mechanism; raised ICP is not the main problem after arrest.
“Hypothermia selectively inhibits apoptosis with little effect on inflammation or free radicals”
It suppresses inflammation and oxidative injury too (PCA-22); ‘selectively’ is the wrong word.
decode: Which statement best describes the rationale for hypothermia’s neuroprotective effect? [DocT]
The option listing several pathways together: reperfusion injury, excitatory neurotransmitters, blood-brain barrier (50% right).
Rationale for therapeutic hypothermia after VF arrest? [Marrow]
Reduced cerebral oxygen consumption.
explain.punch: Cooling protects the post-arrest brain by slowing many processes at once: metabolism and oxygen use, glutamate release, calcium overload and apoptosis; any option that credits one mechanism alone is wrong.

steps.q:
**Trace how TTM practice changed across the evidence:**
a What the early trials showed
b What TTM 2013 showed
c What TTM2 showed
d What the ERC/ESICM 2021 position therefore is
e The one temperature principle that survives all of it
steps.a:
**Stage** | **Finding**
**Early trials** | **Hypothermia BETTER than normothermia** - favourable outcome roughly doubled
**TTM 2013** | **36°C is AS GOOD AS 33°C** - the depth of cooling does not matter
**TTM2** | **Hypothermia is NO BETTER than normothermia**, and causes more arrhythmia
**ERC/ESICM 2021** | **TTM at 36°C**; constant temperature **32-36°C** for ≥24 h; **PREVENT FEVER for at least 72 h**
**ERC-ESICM 2025** | **Actively PREVENT FEVER: ≤37.5°C for 36-72 h**; the constant 32-36°C target is dropped; mild hypothermia (32-36°C) is not actively rewarmed
**AHA 2025** | **Temperature control for AT LEAST 36 HOURS** in patients unresponsive to verbal commands; **goal 32-37.5°C**. Hypothermic (32-34°C) and normothermic / fever-prevention (36-37.5°C) are BOTH 'temperature control'
- **What survives: FEVER IS HARMFUL** (PCA-27). The debate was only ever about how far BELOW normal to go
bank_lines: DocT: No RCT shows that earlier cooling helps: prehospital cold-saline cooling (Kim, JAMA 2014, n=1,359; RINSE) gave no survival or neurological benefit and caused more re-arrest and pulmonary oedema.

explain.sub: Post-arrest care → Evidence → How practice changed: hypothermia to fever prevention
explain.intro: Step 2 summed up. The evidence moved from ‘cool to 32–34 °C’ to ‘control temperature and never let it rise’, and the bank keys lag behind. Three linked questions: two DocT keys are historical or disputed, so the exam-day answer depends on which era the options come from.
why: **Early trials: hypothermia better than normothermia; favourable outcome roughly doubled.** HACA and Bernard (PCA-23) produced the 2002–2010 recommendation of 32–34 °C for 12–24 hours after VF arrest. That is the DocT QBank key (32–34 °C), right for its era and only 57% chose it.
**TTM 2013: 36 °C is as good as 33 °C; the depth of cooling does not matter.** Guidelines widened to a constant 32–36 °C.

**TTM2: hypothermia is no better than normothermia, and causes more arrhythmia.** This was the decisive trial; CAPITAL CHILL (31 vs 34 °C, 2021) also found that deeper cooling did not help and lengthened ICU stay.

**ERC/ESICM 2021: TTM at 36 °C; constant 32–36 °C for ≥24 h; prevent fever for at least 72 h.** The 2021 guideline (published before TTM2) did say: keep a constant 32–36 °C for at least 24 hours and avoid fever above 37.7 °C for at least 72 hours; it did not single out 36 °C. After TTM2, the 2022 ERC–ESICM update dropped the 32–36 °C target and kept only fever prevention (>37.7 °C) for at least 72 hours. ERC–ESICM 2025 now says: actively prevent fever at ≤37.5 °C for 36–72 hours, and do not actively rewarm mild spontaneous hypothermia (32–36 °C).

**What survives: fever is harmful (PCA-27); the debate was only about how far below normal to go.** AHA 2025 calls it temperature control: a deliberate protocol for any adult not following commands after ROSC, any rhythm and any location, at 32–37.5 °C (COR 1) for at least 36 hours (COR 2a). Routine prehospital cooling with rapid cold IV fluid is COR 3, no benefit.
mimic: Hypothermic vs normothermic temperature control
Both are ‘temperature control’ in AHA 2025: 32–34 °C or 36–37.5 °C; what is not allowed is fever.
traps: “Target for VF OHCA is 32–34 °C” as the only correct range
That is the 2002–2010 answer (DocT key). If a 32–37.5 °C or fever-prevention option is offered, choose it; if the options are only historical ranges, 32–34 °C is the keyed one.
“Delaying initiation of TH increases mortality” (DocT key, 47–50% right)

No RCT shows that faster cooling helps; prehospital cold saline after ROSC (Kim, JAMA 2014, 1,359 patients) gave no benefit and more re-arrest and pulmonary oedema, and cold saline during CPR (RINSE, 2016) lowered ROSC in shockable rhythms. The key rests on old observational data, but it is the least wrong option: the others are clearly false (not all arrests; 24 not 48 h; shivering is harmful).
“34 °C is wrong” after a VF OHCA (Marrow key 34 °C)
34 °C sits inside AHA’s 32–37.5 °C range, so it is acceptable when the question follows AHA; if it follows ERC, pick normothermia with fever prevention.
decode: Recommended target temperature after out-of-hospital VF arrest? [DocT]
Keyed 32–34 °C (historical); current AHA 32–37.5 °C (57% right).
Which statement about therapeutic hypothermia is correct? [DocT]
Keyed ‘delaying initiation increases mortality’; the others are plainly wrong (47% right).
Comatose after VF OHCA, absent brainstem reflexes — next step? [Marrow]
Temperature control (keyed 34 °C); brain death cannot be declared this early after arrest.
explain.punch: Practice moved from cooling to 32–34 °C to simply controlling temperature (AHA 32–37.5 °C for at least 36 hours, ERC–ESICM ≤37.5 °C): the only conclusion that has survived every trial is that fever harms.

steps.q:
**For the practical conduct of TTM, give:**
a The phases and their durations
b The nature of the rewarming phase
c What TTM involves, in three parts
d The stated preference
steps.a:
- **AHA 2025:** if not following commands, deliberate temperature control at **32–37.5 °C** (COR 1) for **at least 36 h** (COR 2a); **controlled rewarming no faster than 0.5 °C/h** (COR 2b)
- **ERC-ESICM 2025:** actively prevent fever (target **≤37.5 °C**) for **36–72 h**; do not actively rewarm mild hypothermia (32–36 °C)
- There is no fixed 24 h + 24 h schedule
- TTM involves: **careful monitoring of temperature with an INVASIVE temperature probe** • **targeting a safe temperature** • **coordinated MULTIMODAL control of shivering**
- **It is always preferable to PREVENT fever and shivering, if possible**
bank_lines: DocT: Rewarm after temperature control at ≤0.25–0.5 °C/h: fast rewarming raises cerebral metabolic demand in a brain with fragile O2 delivery, causes vasodilatory hypotension and REBOUND HYPERkalaemia as K+ moves back out of cells (option C has the direction wrong). Afterdrop (D) is an accidental-hypothermia phenomenon.

DocT GT: Temperature control is for comatose survivors after ROSC (not every arrest); hypothermia is held for 24 h (not 48), shivering must be suppressed, and earlier initiation is linked to better outcome. Current ERC-ESICM practice is active fever prevention (≤37.5–37.7 °C) for at least 72 h.

explain.sub: Post-arrest care → Conduct → Phases, duration and rewarming
explain.intro: Step 3 turns the evidence into a protocol. The phases are induction, maintenance, controlled rewarming and then fever prevention, and the two linked questions test why rewarming must be slow and which statements about cooling are true.
why: **AHA 2025: deliberate temperature control at 32–37.5 °C (COR 1) for at least 36 h (COR 2a). ERC–ESICM 2025: prevent fever (≤37.5 °C) for 36–72 h; do not actively rewarm mild hypothermia (32–36 °C). There is no fixed 24 h + 24 h schedule.** The older teaching of 24 hours at target then 24 hours of rewarming has gone; the trials actually ran 72 hours of temperature management in all, and AHA calls 36 hours the minimum.

**Rewarming is controlled, no faster than 0.5 °C/h (AHA COR 2b).** Rapid rewarming raises cerebral metabolic demand abruptly in a brain whose oxygen delivery is still fragile, causes vasodilatation and hypotension, and lets potassium move back out of cells (rebound hyperkalaemia; PCA-38). TTM2 rewarmed at about 0.33 °C/h, HYPERION at 0.25–0.5 °C/h.

**TTM involves: an invasive core temperature probe, a safe target, and coordinated multimodal shivering control.** Bladder or oesophageal probes (PCA-33) feed the device’s feedback loop; shivering control is the tier system (PCA-34–36).

**It is always preferable to prevent fever and shivering, if possible.** Preventing is easier than reversing: once a fever or shivering has started, more drugs and deeper sedation are needed, and those cloud neuroprognostication.
mimic: Controlled rewarming after TTM vs rewarming in accidental hypothermia
Afterdrop (core temperature falling further as cold peripheral blood returns) is an accidental-hypothermia phenomenon during field rewarming; it is not the reason for slow rewarming after TTM.
traps: “Slow rewarming prevents a rapid fall in potassium”
The direction is wrong: rewarming moves potassium out of cells, so the risk is hyperkalaemia (option C).
“Rapid rewarming causes a paradoxical fall in core temperature”
That describes afterdrop in accidental hypothermia (option D); the answer is the cerebral demand-supply mismatch (only 45% right).
“Temperature goal is 32–36 °C for 48 hours” or “TH is for all cardiac arrests”
Temperature control is for comatose survivors only; the hypothermic phase in the trials was 24–28 h, not 48 h, and AHA now gives 32–37.5 °C for at least 36 h.
“Earlier initiation is linked to better outcome” (in the DocT GT line)
Only observational data say so; prehospital cooling RCTs were negative. It is still the keyed answer when the other options are clearly wrong.
decode: Physiological principle behind slow, controlled rewarming? [DocT]
Rapid rewarming abruptly increases cerebral metabolic demand beyond oxygen delivery (45% right).
Which statement about therapeutic hypothermia is correct? [DocT GT]
Keyed ‘delaying initiation increases mortality’ (50% right); the others are wrong on indication, duration and shivering.
explain.punch: Temperature control runs for at least 36 hours at 32–37.5 °C (or ≤37.5 °C in Europe) and ends with rewarming no faster than 0.5 °C/h, because fast rewarming raises brain oxygen demand, drops the pressure and releases potassium.

**Give the advantage of each cooling method:**
a Endovascular
b Infused crystalloids
c Hydrogel-coated pads
d Water circulating pads
e Ice packs
steps.a:
**Method** | **Advantage**
**Endovascular** | **FASTEST cooling possible**
**Infused crystalloids** | **Very fast cooling, easily accessible, WORKS WITH OTHER METHODS**
**Hydrogel-coated pads** | **Very easy to use; rapid cooling AND rewarming**
**Water circulating pads** | **TARGETED NECK (cerebral) cooling possible**; less expensive than invasive methods
**Ice packs** | **Very inexpensive**
bank_lines: DocT GT: Transnasal evaporative cooling (RhinoChill) is the only brain-selective method — cools via the nasopharynx, works prehospital, few side effects — but induction is slow and it has no feedback control, so it cannot hold a target (PRINCESS: no outcome benefit).

explain.sub: Post-arrest care → Cooling methods → Advantages
explain.intro: Step 4, what each method is good for. The one linked GT question adds a method the card does not list: transnasal evaporative cooling, the only brain-selective one (79% right).
why: **Endovascular: fastest cooling possible.** It also gives the tightest maintenance and controlled rewarming through feedback.
**Infused crystalloids: very fast, easily accessible, works with other methods.** Any ward has cold saline, so it is the bridge until a device is attached; it does not replace one.
**Hydrogel-coated pads: very easy to use; rapid cooling and rewarming.** Non-invasive, with servo control, so they suit units without endovascular catheters.
**Water-circulating pads: targeted neck (cerebral) cooling possible; cheaper than invasive methods.**
mimic: Transnasal evaporative cooling vs water-circulating neck cooling

Transnasal (RhinoChill) cools the brain through the nasopharynx, works prehospital and has few side effects, but induction is slow and it has no feedback, so it cannot hold a target; PRINCESS found no outcome benefit.
traps: “Intravascular cooling is the brain-specific method”
Intravascular cools the whole body; the brain-specific method with slow induction and no feedback is transnasal evaporative cooling.
decode: Cooling method specific to the brain, few side effects, slow induction, no feedback control? [DocT GT]
Transnasal evaporative cooling (79% right).
explain.punch: Endovascular is fastest, cold fluid is the accessible bridge, gel pads are easiest, and only transnasal evaporative cooling targets the brain, at the cost of slow induction and no feedback.

steps.q:
**For Tier-2 anti-shivering therapies, give:**
a The entry criterion
b The physical manoeuvre and why it works
c The two sedative infusions
d The ketamine dose and its rationale
e The magnesium target in both units
f The antiemetic, its dose and frequency
steps.a:
- **Entry: shivering DESPITE Tier-1 therapies**
- **Warming hands and feet** - **tricks the body into feeling warm**
- **Dexmedetomidine and/or propofol infusions**
- **Ketamine infusion 0.2-0.3 mg/kg/hour** (low, analgesic dose)
- **Magnesium targeting a SLIGHTLY ELEVATED level - ~3-4 mg/dL or ~1.2-1.6 mM**
- **Ondansetron 4 mg IV q8h** may be considered
bank_lines: DocT: Skin counter-warming plus magnesium is the first answer for shivering during temperature control because neither sedates nor drops BP; opioid boluses (D) are a later sedating tier, cold saline (A) worsens shivering, and paralysis (B) is the last resort, with EEG.

explain.sub: Post-arrest care → Shivering → Tier 2
explain.intro: Step 5, the middle rung. When Tier 1 fails, counter-warming is added and sedatives with anti-shivering action come in, at the cost of some sedation and hypotension. Four questions are linked, all versions of ‘what comes first’.
why: **Entry: shivering despite Tier 1.** The order matters because each step adds harm; Bedside Shivering Assessment Scale 2 (shivering of the arms or upper body) is the usual point to add sedation.

**Warming the hands and feet: it tricks the body into feeling warm.** The hypothalamus sets shivering from a weighted mix of core and skin temperature, and skin contributes about a fifth; warming the skin lowers the shivering threshold without changing core temperature much. It is cheap and harmless, which is why DocT keys it with magnesium as the first step.

**Dexmedetomidine and/or propofol infusions.** Dexmedetomidine (alpha-2 agonist) lowers the shivering threshold with light sedation, at the price of bradycardia and hypotension; propofol sedates more deeply and lowers BP more.
**Ketamine 0.2–0.3 mg/kg/h (low, analgesic dose).** NMDA antagonism reduces shivering; at this dose it supports the blood pressure rather than lowering it.

**Magnesium to a slightly raised level, about 3–4 mg/dL (1.2–1.6 mmol/L).** The Columbia protocol targets this range from the start; the card’s source reserves it for Tier 2. Either way, magnesium is given before the sedatives.
**Ondansetron 4 mg IV every 8 hours may be considered.** A 5-HT3 antagonist with a modest anti-shivering effect.
mimic: Counter-warming vs active rewarming
Counter-warming heats the skin to stop shivering while the device holds the core temperature; it is not rewarming the patient.
traps: “Dexmedetomidine” when magnesium is offered for ‘least hypotension and sedation’
DocT GT keys dexmedetomidine (71–73% right), but magnesium is lower on the ladder and has less hypotension and sedation; choose magnesium if it is offered and has not been tried.
“Midazolam infusion” or “ketamine bolus” for shivering
Midazolam sedates without much anti-shivering effect and accumulates when cold (PCA-36); ketamine is a low-dose infusion, not a bolus.
“Cold saline” or “paralysis first”
Cold saline worsens shivering; paralysis is Tier 3.
decode: Initial intervention for shivering sparing neurology and haemodynamics? [DocT]
Skin counter-warming plus magnesium (32% right).
Moderate shivering despite passive rewarming; least hypotension and sedation? [DocT GT3/GT4]
Keyed dexmedetomidine; magnesium equally defensible.
Initial intervention [DocT GT6]
Counter-warming plus magnesium (47% right).
explain.punch: Counter-warming and magnesium come before any sedative because they reduce shivering without sedation or hypotension; dexmedetomidine, propofol and low-dose ketamine are the next rung.

steps.q:
**For Tier-3 anti-shivering therapies, give:**
a The entry criterion
b The opioid used, and why it is preferred over the alternative
c The treatment of last resort
d What must be running before paralysis
steps.a:
- **Entry: shivering DESPITE Tier-2 therapies**
- **FENTANYL boluses PRN - SAFER THAN MEPERIDINE**
- **PARALYSIS is the treatment of LAST RESORT**
- Cisatracurium requires **a propofol or midazolam infusion with goal RASS -5** AND **a fentanyl infusion** prior to paralysis
bank_lines: DocT GT: Temperature control slows CYP450 metabolism by roughly 7–22% per °C below 37: midazolam (CYP3A4) and fentanyl accumulate, prolonging sedation and confounding neuroprognostication. Atracurium and cisatracurium (Hofmann elimination/ester hydrolysis) are not CYP-dependent; hydromorphone is glucuronidated.

Marrow: Bedside Shivering Assessment Scale 0–3: 0–1 → counter-warming (skin surface warming); 2 → add sedation/analgesia; 3 (trunk + limbs shaking) → escalate to neuromuscular blockade under deep sedation.

explain.sub: Post-arrest care → Shivering → Tier 3 and paralysis
explain.intro: Step 5’s top rung. Opioid boluses, then paralysis under deep sedation and analgesia, are kept last because they remove the examination you need for prognosis. Four questions are linked, including the drug-metabolism question on what cooling does to the sedatives.
why: **Entry: shivering despite Tier 2.** On the Bedside Shivering Assessment Scale, 3 (shivering of the trunk and all limbs) is the usual trigger for neuromuscular blockade.

**Fentanyl boluses as needed, safer than meperidine (pethidine).** Meperidine is the strongest anti-shivering opioid (it lowers the shivering threshold about twice as much as the vasoconstriction threshold, an effect attributed partly to kappa-opioid and alpha-2 actions), but its metabolite normeperidine lowers the seizure threshold and accumulates in renal failure, and it has serotonergic interactions; in a post-arrest brain prone to seizures that is a poor trade.
**Paralysis is the last resort.** It abolishes shivering completely, but it also hides seizures and myoclonus and removes the neurological examination.

**Before cisatracurium: a propofol or midazolam infusion to RASS −5 and a fentanyl infusion.** A paralysed patient cannot show distress, so deep sedation and analgesia must be running first; continuous EEG is advised because seizures become invisible. Cisatracurium is chosen because Hofmann elimination does not depend on the liver or CYP enzymes.
mimic: Midazolam and fentanyl vs atracurium/cisatracurium and hydromorphone during cooling

Cooling slows CYP450 metabolism by about 7–22% per °C below 37, so midazolam (CYP3A4) and fentanyl accumulate and prolong sedation; atracurium and cisatracurium (Hofmann elimination, ester hydrolysis) and hydromorphone (glucuronidation) do not depend on CYP, although Hofmann elimination itself slows a little in the cold.
traps: “Cooling slows CYP450 metabolism of atracurium”
Atracurium is cleared by Hofmann elimination, not CYP; the concern is midazolam (75% right).
“Raise the target to 36 °C” or “large fluid bolus” for refractory shivering
The next step after counter-warming and magnesium have failed is escalation up the ladder, with NMB and EEG at the top (72% right).
“Hofmann elimination slows hydromorphone or midazolam”
Neither drug is cleared by Hofmann elimination.
decode: Persistent shivering despite counter-warming and magnesium — next step? [DocT]
Neuromuscular blockade with continuous EEG (72% right).
Midazolam, hydromorphone and atracurium during TH — concern? [DocT GT]
Reduced CYP450 metabolism of midazolam, prolonged sedation (75% right).
Shivering of the trunk and all limbs (BSAS 3) — next step? [Marrow]
Neuromuscular blockade, under deep sedation.
explain.punch: Paralysis is the last rung because it hides seizures and the examination, so it is given only on top of deep sedation, analgesia and EEG; cooling also slows CYP450, so midazolam and fentanyl linger and confuse prognosis.

**For biomarkers in**
**neuroprognostication, give:**
a The two biomarkers and the
tissue each is released from
b Which is better studied
c What they are NOT influenced by
d The two time points at which they
are tested

value
steps.a:
**Biomarker** | **Source**
**NSE** | Released following injury from **NEURONS**
**S-100B** | Released following injury from **GLIAL tissue**
- **NSE is BETTER STUDIED**
- **NOT influenced by SEDATIVES and NMBD**
- **Tested at 24 HOURS and 72 HOURS**
- **SERIAL INCREASING values are a better**
**predictor than a single value**
- **AHA 2025 addition:** **NEUROFILAMENT LIGHT**
**CHAIN (NfL)** is now included as a serum biomarker
for neuroprognostication
bank_lines: DocT GT: NSE is also present in red cells and platelets, so a HAEMOLYSED sample (or haemolysis on ECMO) gives a falsely high NSE; check free Hb before prognosticating. S-100B (glia) and NfL are not raised by haemolysis in the same way.

DocT GT: Neurofilament light chain is a structural protein of large myelinated AXONS, so raised CSF/serum NfL means axonal injury; it rises even after repetitive mild TBI (boxers). Contrast: NSE = neuronal cell body, S-100B/GFAP = glia/astrocytes.

explain.sub: Neuroprognostication → Biomarkers → NSE, S-100B and NfL
explain.intro: Step 4 turns to blood tests, the one modality that sedatives and paralytics cannot fake. Both GT5 questions test the cell each marker comes from and what else raises it.
why: **NSE is released following injury from neurones; S-100B from glial tissue.** Neurone-specific enolase is a glycolytic enzyme in neuronal cytoplasm, so it leaks when neurones die. S-100B is a calcium-binding protein of astrocytes. NSE is also present in red cells and platelets, which is why haemolysis raises it falsely; ERC–ESICM 2025 says measure free haemoglobin and discard haemolysed samples (relevant on ECMO).
**NSE is better studied.** It is the only biomarker in the ERC–ESICM algorithm (PCA-53). ERC–ESICM 2025 does not recommend S-100B, because thresholds are inconsistent.
**Not influenced by sedatives and NMBD.** This is their value: the clinical examination and most of the EEG are confounded by exactly those drugs (PCA-43).
**Tested at 24 hours and 72 hours.** ERC–ESICM 2025 advises serial samples at 24, 48 and 72 h; the threshold in the algorithm is read at 48 and/or 72 h (PCA-48).

**Serial increasing values are a better predictor than a single value. AHA 2025 addition: neurofilament light chain (NfL) is now included as a serum biomarker for neuroprognostication.** A rise from 24 to 48 h means continuing neuronal death; a falling value suggests a one-off release or haemolysis. NfL is a cytoskeletal protein of large myelinated axons, so it marks axonal injury (GT5 boxer question). AHA 2025 allows high NSE or NfL within 72 h (COR 2b), but ERC–ESICM 2025 does not recommend NfL yet because no consistent threshold exists.
mimic: NSE vs NfL
NSE: neuronal cell body, falsely raised by haemolysis. NfL: axonal structure, also raised in traumatic and neurodegenerative injury.
traps: “Raised NfL in a boxer means glial scarring or blood-brain barrier closure”
NfL is axonal; glial injury is S-100B or GFAP (GT5, 69% right).
“S-100B is the biomarker falsely raised by haemolysis”
It is NSE, because red cells contain enolase (GT5, 71% right).
decode: Raised CSF neurofilament light chain after repeated bouts suggests? [DocT GT]
Axonal injury (69% right).
Neuronal injury marker known for false positives from haemolysis? [DocT GT]
NSE (71% right).
explain.punch: NSE comes from neurones (and red cells, so haemolysis fakes it), S-100B from glia and NfL from axons; biomarkers are useful because no drug alters them, and a rising series counts more than one value.
