steps.a:
| **Findings and timing**
**MRI** | **MORE SENSITIVE**. **DWI**, measure **ADC**. **Hyperintensity in CORTEX and BASAL** **GANGLIA**. **Do at 2-7 DAYS after arrest**
**CT** | **Early CT can already show a reduced grey-white ratio; if the first CT is normal and the patient is still unconscious, REPEAT at 72-96 h**
bank_lines: DocT GT: DWI-MRI is timed after temperature control and sedation clear: too early, DWI underestimates injury; too late (beyond ~1 week), ADC changes pseudo-normalise.

explain.sub: Neuroprognostication → Imaging → CT vs MRI
explain.intro: Step 4, imaging. CT shows swelling, MRI shows dying cells, and each has a window. The GT1o day-6 question (41% right) is keyed on MRI, and GT6 asks the MRI day window.
why: **MRI is more sensitive.** Diffusion-weighted imaging detects cytotoxic oedema (cells swelling as their ion pumps fail) before the tissue changes density on CT.

**DWI, measure ADC.** Restricted diffusion appears bright on DWI and dark on the ADC map; a low ADC confirms true restriction rather than T2 ‘shine-through’. AHA 2025 accepts extensive restricted diffusion or reduced ADC at 2–7 days.

**Hyperintensity in cortex and basal ganglia.** The cortex (especially occipital and the perirolandic areas), basal ganglia, thalamus and hippocampus have the highest metabolic demand and fail first. GT1o’s key is ‘MRI can assist, and the cortex is the most commonly affected area’.

**MRI at 2–7 days after arrest; early CT can show reduced grey-white ratio; if the first CT is normal and the patient is still unconscious, repeat at 72–96 h.** Before day 2 diffusion changes may not have appeared fully; after about a week the ADC pseudo-normalises and injury is underestimated. AHA 2025 and ERC–ESICM 2025 both use 2–7 days; ERC–ESICM 2021 said 2–5 days. The repeat CT at 72–96 h is ERC–ESICM 2025.
mimic: CT vs MRI after arrest
CT: early, quick, shows oedema and lost grey-white ratio, low sensitivity early. MRI: 2–7 days, more sensitive, shows cytotoxic injury.
traps: “EEG is the most accurate prognostic test” (GT1o option A)
No single test is ‘the most accurate’; bilateral absent N20 is the most specific one.
“No corneal responses at day 6 means no recovery” (option B)
Corneal absence alone is not enough: ERC needs absent pupillary AND corneal reflexes plus a second criterion.
“NSE can be used at day 6” (option C)

The guideline threshold is set for 48 h and/or 72 h; a day-6 value is outside the window the cut-off was validated for, and temperature control can alter NSE kinetics, so ‘not affected by cooling’ is also too strong.
“MRI immediately after arrest” or ‘days 2–5 only’ (GT6)

Too early shows nothing. DocT keys days 3–7 (69% right). The 2025 guidelines say 2–7 days; 2–5 days is ERC–ESICM 2021. Pick 2–7 if offered. With these four options, pick DocT’s 3–7 (inside the current 2–7 window); choose 2–5 only if the stem is explicitly framed on ERC–ESICM 2021.
decode: Post-arrest day 6, limited recovery: which is most correct? [DocT GT]
MRI can assist with prognosis, and the cortex is the most commonly affected region (41% right).
On what day is MRI brain advised after cardiac arrest? [DocT GT]
Key: days 3–7 (69% right); guideline window 2–7 days.
explain.punch: CT is early and shows swelling; diffusion MRI at 2–7 days is more sensitive and shows restriction in the cortex and basal ganglia; repeat a normal early CT at 72–96 hours if the patient is still unconscious.

**arrest, give:**

oedema

steps.a:
- **Cerebral oedema: around 50% incidence**
- **ATTENUATION OF THE GREY-WHITE MATTER**
**INTERFACE**
bank_lines: Marrow: Diffuse hypoattenuation with lost grey–white differentiation after arrest = global anoxic injury: there is no surgical role, so the step is multimodal prognostication and counselling the family, not a neurosurgical referral.

explain.sub: Neuroprognostication → Imaging → CT findings
explain.intro: Step 4, what the CT shows. Global hypoxia swells the grey matter until it looks like white matter. The Marrow hanging question tests what that means for management.
why: **Cerebral oedema: around 50% incidence.** Reported rates vary widely with how long after arrest the CT is done; early CT is often normal, which is why a negative first scan is repeated (PCA-49).

**Attenuation of the grey-white matter interface.** Grey matter (cortex, basal ganglia) uses more energy, so it swells first; its density falls towards that of white matter, the boundary fades and sulci and cisterns efface. A reduced grey-white ratio is the measurable form; ERC–ESICM 2025 uses a marked reduction, and repeats a normal early CT at 72–96 h if the patient is still unconscious.
mimic: Global anoxic injury vs focal stroke or haematoma
Anoxic injury is diffuse and symmetrical with no mass to remove; a focal lesion may have a surgical answer.
traps: “Neurosurgical consult” for diffuse loss of grey-white differentiation after hanging
There is no surgical target; the step is multimodal prognostication and counselling the family (Marrow).
decode: Hanging, GCS 3, CT loss of grey-white differentiation: diagnosis and step? [Marrow]
Anoxic brain injury; family education and prognostication, not surgery.
explain.punch: Diffuse loss of grey-white differentiation on CT means global anoxic injury with nothing to operate on, so the response is prognostication and honest discussion with the family.

explain.intro: Step 6 lays out the whole road from ROSC, of which prognostication is only one branch. Both Marrow questions sit on it: residual sedation, and donation after circulatory death.
why: **Unresponsive patient after ROSC: suspected neurological cause of arrest?** Subarachnoid haemorrhage, stroke or trauma can cause the arrest; finding it changes everything that follows.
**Yes: brain CT.** Before temperature control, to find a lesion that needs a different treatment.

**No: TTM, then unresponsive after rewarming, then exclude confounders, particularly residual sedation.** Temperature control goes to every comatose survivor; sedation delays the examination, not the cooling.
**All brainstem reflexes absent? Pupillary, corneal, oculocephalic, cough.** These test the midbrain, pons and medulla in turn.

**Yes: brain death pathway. No: neuroprognostication, WLST at any time, then evaluate for organ donation; circulatory death at any time, then evaluate for organ donation.** AHA 2025 (COR 1): consider organ donation in every patient who meets brain death criteria and before planned WLST. Donation after circulatory death: the treating team withdraws treatment, circulatory death follows, a no-touch period of a few minutes, then retrieval; the donation team never leads the WLST decision.
mimic: Donation after brain death vs after circulatory death
Brain death donors are dead by neurological criteria with the heart beating; circulatory death donors die after planned WLST.
traps: “Comatose on propofol and fentanyl with pinpoint pupils: neither temperature control option is indicated yet” (Marrow key)

Disputed: AHA and ERC give temperature control to all comatose survivors. Sedation delays prognosis and brain death testing, not temperature control. If asked about starting temperature control, start it; if about prognosis, wait for sedation to clear.
“The donation team should lead the withdrawal discussion”
WLST is decided and carried out by the treating team; donation is raised separately.
decode: Post-OHCA on propofol/fentanyl, GCS 3T, pinpoint pupils: what next? [Marrow]
Key ‘neither TTM option yet’ (disputed); the real point is that sedation must clear before any neurological judgement.
Severe TBI, not brain dead, family requests withdrawal: management? [Marrow]
Offer donation after circulatory death.
explain.punch: Suspect a neurological cause and scan first; otherwise control temperature, rewarm and clear sedation, then check the brainstem: all reflexes absent leads to brain death testing, some present to prognostication, and organ donation is considered on every branch.

bank_lines: Marrow: Clinical brain-death criteria: coma of known irreversible cause, absent brainstem reflexes, positive apnoea test (no breathing at PaCO2 ≥60 or ≥20 above baseline in CO2 retainers, pH <7.30); spinal reflexes may persist. Prerequisites: core temperature ≥36 °C, SBP ≥100 (vasopressors allowed), eucapnia at start, no confounding drugs; locked-in syndrome is a mimic.

explain.sub: Neuroprognostication → Algorithm → Brain death limb
explain.intro: Step 6, the other road. When the whole brain including the brainstem has stopped working, the question is no longer outcome but death. Marrow asks which criteria can declare it.
why: **Signs of brain death: fixed dilated pupils, diabetes insipidus, cardiovascular changes.** Hypothalamic and posterior pituitary failure stops ADH release, so polyuria and hypernatraemia follow; loss of brainstem control causes a catecholamine surge, then vasoplegia and hypotension.
**CT: severe cerebral oedema and brainstem herniation.** This is the CT that turns the question from prognosis to brain death testing.

**Follow the World Brain Death Project recommendations.** The 2020 consensus: coma of known irreversible cause, absent brainstem reflexes and a positive apnoea test (no breathing when PaCO₂ reaches ≥60 mmHg with pH <7.30, or ≥20 mmHg above baseline in chronic CO₂ retainers), after prerequisites (core temperature ≥36 °C, systolic ≥100 mmHg or MAP ≥60 mmHg, no confounding drugs, at least five half-lives of the longest-acting sedative). Spinal reflexes may persist. EEG and blood-flow studies are ancillary, used when the clinical examination cannot be completed.
**Brain death confirmed according to local legislation.** The criteria are international; the declaration is local (in India, under the Transplantation of Human Organs Act, by a board of doctors).
mimic: Brain death vs locked-in syndrome
Locked-in patients are conscious with vertical eye movements and blinking preserved; a ventral pontine lesion, not loss of the whole brain.
traps: “An isoelectric EEG is required to declare brain death”
The diagnosis is clinical; EEG is ancillary. Marrow’s key (isoelectric EEG, absent brainstem reflexes, positive apnoea test) lists what can be used, not what is mandatory.
“Preserved spinal reflexes exclude brain death”
They may persist because the spinal cord is intact.
decode: Which criteria can be used to declare brain death? [Marrow]
Absent brainstem reflexes and a positive apnoea test in coma, with isoelectric EEG as an ancillary test.
explain.punch: Brain death is a clinical diagnosis of coma, absent brainstem reflexes and a positive apnoea test once confounders are excluded; diabetes insipidus is one of its signs, EEG is ancillary and the declaration follows local law.

explain.sub: Post-cardiac arrest care → Neuroprognostication → AHA 2025 additions
explain.intro: Step 3 ends with prognosis, where 2025 made the assessment two-sided. Until 2020 every test looked only for signs of a poor outcome; now the guideline also lists signs of a good one. The two DocT Grand Test questions ask what NfL means and when to decide.
why: **The section now includes predictors of FAVOURABLE outcome, not only of poor outcome.** A continuous EEG background, a normal NSE (<17 µg/L at 24–72 h) and a withdrawal or better motor response (each 2b) may support a good outcome. Preserved pupillary or corneal reflexes do not (3: No Benefit), because many patients with them still do badly.

**NEUROFILAMENT LIGHT CHAIN (NfL) added as a serum biomarker.** NfL is a structural protein of large myelinated axons, so a raised serum or CSF level means axonal injury; it rises after any axonal damage, including repeated mild head injury in boxers. After arrest, high NfL (or NSE) within 72 hours may support a poor outcome (2b) when combined with other tests; no threshold is set and assays differ. NSE marks neuronal cell bodies, S-100B and GFAP mark glia.

**A continuous EEG background WITHOUT DISCHARGES within 72 h supports a FAVOURABLE prognosis, when interpreted with other tests.** A continuous, reactive background with no epileptiform discharges indicates a functioning cortex. This is the reverse of the poor-outcome EEG signs (burst suppression or suppression without sedation at ≥72 h).

**Treatment to suppress myoclonus WITHOUT an EEG correlate is NOT recommended — no evidence it contributes to secondary brain injury.** 3: No Benefit; get an EEG to separate it from seizures (ACLS-61e).

**Multimodal approach with delayed impressions: consolidate at ≥72 hours after NORMOTHERMIA and discontinuation of sedatives (class 2a).** No single sign decides (1), impressions are delayed (1), and the assessment is consolidated at least 72 hours after normothermia and off sedation (2a). The 72-hour rule was already in 2020; 2025 restates it. Hypothermia slows drug clearance and itself depresses reflexes, so an early examination during cooling overestimates injury.
mimic: NfL vs NSE vs S-100B/GFAP
Axons vs neuronal cell bodies vs glia.
Favourable vs unfavourable EEG
Continuous background without discharges vs burst suppression or suppression off sedation.
traps: “Day 2 of cooling, absent corneal reflexes: withdraw” (83% right)
Hypothermia and sedation confound the examination; wait at least 72 hours after normothermia.
“Send NSE now to guide immediate prognosis”
No single marker decides, and none is acted on before 72 hours.
“Raised NfL means glial scarring or BBB closure” (69% right)
NfL is axonal; glial injury is marked by S-100B and GFAP.
decode: Amateur boxer with raised CSF NfL — what does it suggest? [DocT GT, 69%]
Axonal injury.
Post-arrest, cooled, day 2: absent corneal reflexes, no pain response — next step in prognostication? [DocT GT, 83%]
Wait at least 72 hours before deciding.
explain.punch: Prognostication in 2025 waits at least 72 hours after normothermia, combines several tests, and now looks for signs of recovery as well as of damage, so it can argue for continuing as well as for stopping.
